Surah 75: Al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection). It is Meccan, and its verses number forty.

﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection.﴾

The entry of the negative "lā" (no/not) before the verb of oath is common, and its benefit is to emphasise the oath. The scholars said: it is a superfluous particle (ṣilah), like it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that the People of the Book may not know﴾. It was also said: it is for negation, but "lā" negates not the act of swearing itself; rather the negation points to the magnitude and exaltation of the one sworn by. As if the meaning of "I do not swear by such-and-such" is: I do not glorify it by swearing by it as its due glorification requires, for it deserves far more than that. As for what was said, that the meaning is the negation of swearing because the matter is clear, you already know what is wrong with it from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾. It was also said: "lā" is a negation addressed to a statement that preceded the oath, as if they had denied the resurrection, so it was said: "Nay," meaning the matter is not as they claim. Then it was said: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection," like your saying: "No, by God, the resurrection is true." Whichever of these views is correct, there is in swearing to the certainty of the resurrection by the Day of Resurrection a grandeur beyond which there is no greater. Its detailed treatment has already passed in the commentary on Surah Yasin and Surah al-Zukhruf.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 2:

﴿And I do not swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾. That is: by the pious soul that blames the (other) souls on that Day for their shortcomings in piety. Thus there is in this a share of the eloquence found in the preceding oath. Or: by the soul that blames itself, even if it has striven in acts of obedience. Or: by the tranquil soul that reproaches the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah). It has also been said: it refers to the category (of souls), on the basis of what is related that he (ﷺ) said: "There is no soul, righteous or wicked, but that it will blame itself on the Day of Resurrection: if it did good, it says, 'Why did I not increase (it)?' and if it did evil, it says, 'Would that I had fallen short.'" Its weakness is not hidden, for this degree of blame does not serve as a ground for magnifying (something) by swearing an oath by it, even if it issues from a believing soul that does wrong; how then (could it be so) from a disbelieving soul, which falls under the category? It has also been said: it refers to the soul of Adam (peace be upon him), for it continues to blame itself over the act because of which it was expelled from the Garden. The answer to the oath is what is indicated by the words of the Exalted:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 3:**

﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ Its meaning is: "He will certainly be resurrected." By "man" is meant the species. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denial of what has occurred and for condemning it. "*An*" is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), which is its subject, is omitted. Its meaning is: "Does he think that the matter is that We will not assemble his bones?" For that supposition is false, since We do assemble them after they have scattered and become decayed (*ramīm*) and crumbled (*rufāt*), mixed with the dust, after the winds have swept them away and scattered them across the regions of the earth, and cast them into the seas. It is said that 'Udayy ibn Abi Rabi'ah, the brother-in-law (*khatan*) of al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, and they are the two of whom the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to say: "O Allah, suffice me against my bad neighbour," said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will it occur, and what is its matter like?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed him, and he said: "If I were to witness that day, I would not believe you, or [until] Allah gathers these bones."

Yes, indeed. We shall gather them, while We are **able to level/restore his fingertips** (bananahu). That is, we gather his small bones (sulamiyyat) and join some of them to others, just as they were with their smallness and fineness; so how much more so the great bones?

Or it means: **We are able to level his fingers**, which are his extremities and the last thing with which his creation is completed. And it is recited as (qadirun) [in the nominative].

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 5:

﴿Nay, man wishes to continue in sin before him.﴾ It is conjoined (ʿatf) to "Does man think..." (ayahsabu), either on the basis that it is itself an interrogative like it, in which case it turns away from the rebuke expressed by that to the rebuke expressed by this; or on the basis that it is an affirmative statement to which one has shifted from the interrogative, meaning: "Nay, he wishes to persist in his immorality throughout the times that lie before him and the time that he will encounter, not refraining from it."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 6:**

﴿He asks: When will the Day of Resurrection come?﴾ That is: when will it occur, asked either in disbelief at its occurrence or in mockery.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 7:

"So when the sight is dazzled" — i.e., bewildered with terror, from "baraqa al-rajul" (the man was dazzled), when one looks at lightning and his sight is struck with amazement. It is also read with a fatha on the ra' (barqa), which is a dialectal form (lughah). Or it is from al-bariq (glittering), in the sense of "lamaʿa" (it flashed), due to the intensity of its staring (shukhus). It is also read "baliqa" (balaqa), i.e., it opened wide and was split apart.
﴿And the moon will be darkened﴾: that is, its light will go away. It is also read in the passive voice, "khusifa" (خُسِفَ).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 9:**

﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ — by Allah, exalted is He, causing them to rise from the west. And it has been said: they are joined in the loss of their light. And it has been said: they will be brought together black and folded up, as if they were two bulls thrown down and burning in the fire. And the verb is masculine in form because it precedes its subject, and because the conjoined noun is given precedence (taghlib al-ma'tuf).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 10:

﴿Man will say on that Day﴾, that is, on the day when these matters take place, ﴿"Where is the place of escape?"﴾ That is, the flight (al-firar), in despair of it. It is also read with a kasra (al-Mafirr), meaning the place of flight. It has been permitted that it may also be a verbal noun (masdar) like al-marji' (the return).

(p-66) ﴿Kalla﴾ (No!), a rebuke against his seeking refuge and wishing for escape. ﴿La wazar﴾ (There is no refuge): no place of shelter, a metaphor drawn from a mountain. It is said: "Every thing you take refuge in and are saved by is your wazar (refuge)."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 12:

﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the place of rest.﴾ That is: to Him alone is the resting-place of the servants. Or: to His judgment is the settling of their affair. Or: to His will is the place of their abode; He admits whomever He wills to Paradise, and whomever He wills to Hellfire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 13:

﴿He will be informed, on that Day, the human being﴾ That is: every person, whether righteous or wicked, will be informed at the weighing of deeds ﴿of what he sent forward﴾ That is: what he did of deeds, whether good or evil; so he will be rewarded for the first and punished for the second ﴿and kept back﴾ That is: what he did not do, whether good or evil; so he will be punished for the first and rewarded for the second. Or it means: what he sent forward of good or bad deeds, and what he kept back of a good or bad sunnah (practice) that was then acted upon after him; or what he sent forward of wealth that he gave in charity during his life, and what he kept back, so that his heirs take it, or he endowed it as a waqf (endowment), or bequeathed it; or it means the first of his deeds and the last of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 14:

﴿Nay, man is a clear witness against himself﴾. That is: a proof and evidence against himself, a witness to the evil deeds that proceeded from him, as is indicated by the word "عَلى" ('alā, "against") and by the circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah) that comes later. It is described with insight (baṣīrah) figuratively, just as the signs are described with sight in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So when Our signs came to them, clear to see﴾. Or it is "ʿayn baṣīrah" (a seeing eye). Or the tā' is for emphasis (mubālaghah). The meaning of "بَلْ" (bal, "nay") is progression (tarraqqī). That is: man is informed of his deeds; nay, on that Day he is knowing of the details of his states and a witness against himself, because his limbs speak to that. And His words, Exalted is He:

﴿Even if he should offer his excuses.﴾ That is: even if he came with every excuse by which he could defend himself. (*Hal*, a circumstantial accusative, is a grammatical term meaning a word in the accusative that describes the state of another noun.) It is a *hal* from the hidden pronoun in *baseerah* (the hidden pronoun in the word *baseerah*), or from the *marfu'* (nominative noun) in *yunabba'* (is informed). That is, he is a *baseerah* (a witness) against himself: his own limbs will testify against him, and their testimony will be accepted even if he offers every excuse. Or, he is informed of his deeds, even if he offers excuses... and so on. *Al-ma'adhir* (the excuses) is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) for *al-ma'dhirah* (an excuse), just as *al-manakir* is a collective noun for *al-munkar* (the wrong). It has also been said that it is the plural of *mi'dhar* (a curtain), meaning: even if he let down his curtains.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to strive to recite the revelation along with Jibril, peace be upon him, when it was being taught to him. He would not wait until Jibril had finished reciting, in his haste to memorize it and out of fear that it would escape him. So Allah commanded him, peace and blessings be upon him, to listen attentively, directing his heart and hearing towards it until the revelation was completed for him. Then the revelation is completed for him, and then Allah makes him follow it with study until it becomes firmly fixed in him. So it was said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 16:**

﴿Do not move your tongue with it﴾, i.e., with the Qur'an, ﴿your tongue﴾ at the time of the descent of the Revelation.

﴿So that you may hasten with it﴾, i.e., so that you may take it in haste, out of fear that it might slip away from you.
(p-67) ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection﴾ in your breast, such that none of its meanings escapes you, ﴿and its recitation﴾, i.e., establishing its recitation on your tongue.

﴿Then when We recite it﴾, i.e., We complete its recitation to you through the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him. The attribution of the recitation to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah, the royal "We") is for emphasis on the obligation of deliberateness. ﴿Then follow its recitation﴾, so be one who follows it closely, and do not rush ahead of it.
Then, indeed, upon Us is its explanation (Qur'an 75:19). That is: the explanation of whatever in its meanings and rulings has become unclear to you.

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rebuke to him, peace and blessings be upon him, for his habit of haste, and an encouragement to him toward deliberation. He emphasized this with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but you love the fleeting life﴾.

"And you leave the Hereafter" — addressed generally to all, meaning: rather, you, O children of Adam, since you were created from haste and were made disposed to it, hasten toward everything; and for this reason you love the immediate (ʿājila) and leave the Hereafter (al-ākhira). It was also said that "kallā" (nay/no) is a rebuke to man against being deceived by the immediate, so that the plural pronoun in the two verbs is taken in consideration of the meaning of the genus (jins); and this is supported by the reading of the two verbs in the third-person (ghayba) form.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 22:

﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾. That is: many faces, namely the faces of the sincere believers, on the Day when the Resurrection arises, bright and beaming, upon which the radiance of bliss is witnessed. [Grammatically,] "wujuh" (faces) is the subject (mubtada'), "nadiratun" (radiant) is its predicate (khabar), and "yawma'idhin" (on that Day) is in the accusative, governed by "nadiratun." As for "nadhiratun" (looking) in His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 23:

﴿Looking towards their Lord.﴾ It is either a second predicate of the subject, or an attribute of "nāḍiratun" (radiant). "Ilā rabbihā" (towards their Lord) is connected to "nāẓiratun" (looking). The indefinite noun "nāḍiratun" may stand as a subject because the context is one of detailing, not because "nāḍiratun" is an attribute of "wujūhun" (faces) with "nāẓiratun" as the predicate, as some have said, following what is well known: that the rule for an attribute is that its attachment to the described thing should be known to the hearer. Since the radiance of the faces is not established in this way, it is right that it be stated as a predicate. The meaning of their being "looking towards their Lord" is that they see Him, exalted is He, absorbed in contemplating His beauty, to the extent that they forget everything else, and witness Him, exalted is He, without modality and without direction. This is not in all states, such that their looking at something else would contradict it. It has been said that "nāẓiratun" means "awaiting His reward and His bounty." This was refuted on the grounds that waiting is not attributed to a face, that interpreting it by the phrase is contrary to the apparent meaning, and that the verb used in this sense is not transitive with "ilā" (towards).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 24:**

(p-68) ﴿And faces that Day will be scowling﴾, intensely frowning; and these are the faces of the disbelievers.
Tazunnu (تَظُنُّ): their owners expect that a calamity (فاقِرَةٌ, fāqira) will be done to them, a great catastrophe that breaks the spine of the back.

﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke against preferring the fleeting world over the Hereafter. That is, refrain from this and take heed of what lies before you: death, at which the bond between you and the fleeting world is severed.

﴿When it reaches the collarbones﴾ means the soul reaches the upper part of the chest, which are the bones flanking the hollow of the throat on the right and on the left.

﴿And it will be said: "Who is a charmer?"﴾ That is: whoever is present with him (the dying person) says, "Who will perform ruqyah for him and save him from what he is in, of the ruqyah (affliction of death)?" It is also said: this is from the words of the angels of death: "Which of you will ascend with his soul, the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment?" (from ruqi, to ascend).
﴿And he thought that it was the parting﴾. The dying person (al-muhtaḍir) became certain that what had come upon him was the parting from this world and its pleasures.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 29:**

﴿And the leg is wrapped around the leg﴾. His leg becomes entwined with his other leg, and they twist about each other at the arrival of death. It has also been said that they refer to the intensity of parting from the world and the intensity of turning toward the Hereafter. And it has been said that they are his two legs when they are bound together in his shroud.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 30:

﴿To your Lord on that Day is the driving (al-masaq)﴾. That is: to Allah and to His judgment one is driven, not to anyone else.

So he did not affirm what it is obligatory to affirm concerning the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Qur'an that was revealed to him. Or: he did not affirm his wealth, nor did he purify it (give its zakat).

﴿Nor did he pray﴾ what was prescribed for him. The pronoun in both phrases refers to the human being mentioned in His words, ﴿Does man think...﴾. This indicates that the disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings (furu') of the Shari'ah as far as accountability is concerned, as has passed.

﴿But he denied﴾ what was mentioned: the Messenger and the Qur'an.

﴿and turned away﴾ from obedience.

﴿Then he went back to his family, swaggering.﴾ *Yatabakhtaru* (يَتَبَخْتَرُ): he struts with pride, boasting of that. It is from *al-matt* (المَطّ), "stretching," because the one who struts stretches his steps, so its origin is *yatamattatu* (يَتَمَطَّطُ). Or it is from *al-mata* (المَطا), which is the back, because he twists it (يَلْوِيهِ). (p-69)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 34:

﴿Awlā laka fa-awlā﴾ means: woe to you. Its original form is awlāka Allāh mā takrahu ("may God bring upon you what you dislike"), and the lām is extra (ziyādah), as in radifa lakum (the lām being an added particle). Or awlā laka: destruction (al-halāk) is yours. It has also been said that it is af'al (the elative form) from al-wayl (woe), after metathesis (al-qalb), like adnā from dūn. Or it is fa'lā from āla (to return), yaʼūlu, in the sense of: your final outcome ('uqbāka) is the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 35:

﴿Then woe to you, and woe!﴾ That is: this is repeated upon him time after time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 36:

﴿Does man think that he will be left aimless?﴾ That is: left neglected, so that he is not held accountable and is not recompensed. It has also been said: that he will be left in his grave and not be resurrected. And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 37:

﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted (in the womb)?﴾ ... etc. It is a resumptive statement (istі'naf) that comes to refute the reckoning mentioned, for since its basis was their considering resurrection far-fetched, He argued for its certainty by the beginning of creation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 38:

﴿Then he became a clinging clot﴾ i.e., by the power of Allah, Exalted is He, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot﴾. ﴿Then He shaped it﴾ i.e., He determined it by making it a lump of flesh formed (mukhallaqah).

﴿And proportioned it﴾: He made it balanced (fa-'addala) and perfected its creation.

﴿So He made of him﴾ — of man.

﴿the two sexes﴾ — i.e., the two kinds.

﴿the male and the female﴾ — an apposition (badal) to "the two sexes."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 75, verse 40:

﴿Is not That﴾ (the One of great majesty) Who brought into being this wondrous creation?

﴿Able to give life to the dead﴾ — and that is easier than initiating creation, according to the measure of reason.

It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say, when he recited it: "Subhanaka, bala" ("Glory be to You, indeed [You are able]"). And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Qiyamah, I and Jibril will bear witness for him on the Day of Resurrection that he was a believer in the Day of Resurrection."
